extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, counsel handling USPTO reciprocal-discipline matters, and USPTO/OED staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO Director applies under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 to decide whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication (following Selling v. Radford). Covers burdens of proof, permissible defenses (due process, infirmity of proof, grave injustice), and post-discipline obligations and administrative actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from state disbarment / Selling presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: A state disbarment creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper (Selling v. Radford).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO Director begins with the presumption that identical discipline should be imposed unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates one of the Selling/37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible defenses under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall impose identical discipline unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere lacked notice or opportunity to be heard (due process); (ii) there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to a clear conviction that the Office could not accept the conclusion; (iii) imposition would result in a grave injustice; or (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured/reprimanded/placed on probation/disbarred/suspended/disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four enumerated grounds mirror the Selling factors and set the narrow categories in which a respondent may prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid reciprocal discipline the respondent must demonstrate one of the §11.24(d)(1) defenses by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts and the USPTO apply a narrow standard; it is the respondent's burden, and the showing required is difficult. The Office is not a court of review to reweigh evidence or retry factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process deficiency (notice/opportunity to be heard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must clearly and convincingly show substantive procedural deprivation; mere disagreement with outcomes or rulings is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof (insufficient evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not accept the state's conclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must do more than challenge the factfinder's weighing—must show specific, convincing flaws (e.g., identified false evidence, demonstrable factual errors). Conclusory or non-specific allegations are insufficient. Deference is given to credibility findings by the trier-of-fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice (disproportionate sanction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that imposition of the same discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct; courts ask whether the original sanction was so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that imposing it would be unjust. Showing grave injustice requires clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity/character of original discipline (whether publicly imposed)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit ground is whether any argument exists that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent may assert that the state action was not of the type claimed, but must establish that fact by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to state factfinder credibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations by the trier-of-fact regarding witness credibility generally receive deference in reciprocal-discipline proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents must explain why state witness testimony or credibility findings were incorrect; mere disagreement or listing of contrary documents/billing records without confronting testimony is insufficient to overcome deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity requirement for claims of false evidence or statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that false statements or false evidence were used in the state proceeding must be specific (identify particular misleading statements/documents) to show infirmity of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic or conclusory claims that witnesses were 'manipulative' or documents were 'not representative' fail to meet the clear-and-convincing threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal preemption defense (Sperry and Kroll limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that state discipline is preempted by federal law (e.g., federal patent practice) is governed by Sperry v. State of Fla.; state control over law practice within its borders persists except to the limited extent necessary for federal objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline related to federal matters (e.g., patent practice) is not per se preempted; preemption applies only where state action conflicts with federal objectives. Precedent (Kroll) supports that state discipline need not be preempted where it does not attempt to exclude practice before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the USPTO reciprocal sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: If imposed, the Office may order exclusion from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters (i.e., identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director's order will specify effective date and the scope (e.g., exclusion from practice in all USPTO matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline administrative and notice obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If reciprocal discipline is imposed, the OED Director will publish notice in the Official Gazette, notify state disciplinary agencies and courts where practitioner is admitted, and give public notice under 37 C.F.R. § 11.59.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and notification are required steps; disciplinary decisions are made publicly available (e.g., OED FOIA Reading Room).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline practitioner obligations (37 C.F.R. § 11.58 duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplined practitioner must comply with the duties enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order requires the respondent to comply with those regulatory duties (e.g., notices to clients and counsel, although the Order references § 11.58 generally rather than listing each duty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative relief measures (dissociation of Customer Numbers and PKI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may dissociate the respondent's name from any USPTO Customer Numbers and the public key infrastructure (PKI) certificates associated with those Customer Numbers, and prohibit obtaining or being added to a Customer Number until reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders may include administrative restrictions on USPTO systems access and certificate association as part of reciprocal discipline.
